title: Density & Probabilistic Clustering
summary: Clustering beyond K-means — density-based DBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and outliers, and Gaussian Mixture Models for soft, probabilistic cluster assignment.

slides.markdown:
K-means assumes round, similarly-sized clusters. Real data rarely obliges — clusters can be crescents, wildly different densities, or have genuine outliers that don't belong anywhere.

Two methods fix different pieces of that: **DBSCAN** finds clusters by density and calls sparse points noise; **Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs)** give every point a probability of belonging to each cluster instead of a hard yes/no.

slides.subTitle: Density-based clusters and noise
slides.markdown:
**DBSCAN** (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) grows clusters from areas where points are packed densely together, rather than from a fixed number of centroids.

A point is a **core point** if it has enough neighbors within a radius; clusters form by chaining core points together through their neighborhoods. Points that don't belong to any dense region are explicitly labeled **noise** — not forced into the nearest cluster like K-means would do. This makes DBSCAN naturally good at finding oddly-shaped clusters and flagging real outliers.

slides.subTitle: eps and minPts
slides.markdown:
DBSCAN has two parameters, and the whole result hinges on them:

- **eps** — the radius that defines a point's neighborhood.
- **minPts** — how many neighbors (including itself) a point needs within `eps` to count as a core point.

Too small an `eps` splits one real cluster into many; too large merges separate clusters into one blob. A common trick: plot the distance to each point's k-th nearest neighbor sorted ascending, and pick `eps` at the curve's knee.

| | DBSCAN | K-means |
|---|---|---|
| Cluster shape | Arbitrary | Roughly spherical only |
| Needs `k` upfront | No | Yes |
| Handles outliers | Yes — labels them noise | No — every point forced into a cluster |
| Sensitive to | `eps` and `minPts` | Initialization and `k` |
| Varying density across clusters | Struggles | Struggles |

**How to decide:** reach for DBSCAN when you expect irregular shapes or genuine outliers and don't know `k`; reach for K-means when clusters are roughly round and speed on large data matters more.

slides.subTitle: Soft, probabilistic assignment
slides.markdown:
A **Gaussian Mixture Model** assumes the data was generated by a mix of `k` overlapping Gaussian (bell-curve) distributions, each with its own mean, spread, and weight.

Instead of assigning each point to exactly one cluster, a GMM gives every point a **probability** of belonging to each Gaussian — point X might be 70% cluster 1, 30% cluster 2. That soft assignment captures genuine ambiguity near cluster boundaries that a hard K-means split simply erases.

slides.subTitle: How EM fits it
slides.markdown:
A GMM is fit with **Expectation-Maximization (EM)**, which mirrors K-means' assign/update loop but in probabilities:

1. **E-step** — given the current Gaussians, compute each point's probability of belonging to each one.
2. **M-step** — given those probabilities, re-estimate each Gaussian's mean, spread, and weight to best fit the (weighted) points.

Repeat until the probabilities stop changing meaningfully. Like K-means, EM only guarantees a local optimum, so multiple random restarts are standard practice.

slides.subTitle: GMM vs K-means
slides.markdown:
| | GMM (soft) | K-means (hard) |
|---|---|---|
| Assignment | Probability per cluster | One cluster, no ambiguity |
| Cluster shape | Elliptical, any orientation | Spherical |
| Output usable as | Confidence score | Label only |
| Cost | Higher (fits full covariance) | Lower |

**How to decide:** pick GMM when you need a confidence score or clusters are elongated/rotated; pick K-means when you just need a fast, hard label and clusters are roughly round.
